title: Hong Kong Observatory Explains "UFO Cloud" Over Tsing Yi as Lenticular Cloud, Not a Flying Saucer

content:
The Hong Kong Observatory has published a photograph taken over Tsing Yi showing a cloud that resembles a flying saucer. The Observatory clarified that the formation is not a spacecraft, but a lenticular cloud.

The Hong Kong Observatory has published a photograph taken over Tsing Yi showing a cloud that resembles a flying saucer. Photo source: FB@Hong Kong Observatory

According to the Observatory, lenticular clouds are typically produced by orographic lifting. When a layer of relatively stable and moist air is forced to rise over hills or mountains, it sets off up-and-down wave motions in the atmosphere. The rising air within the wave cools the moisture, causing it to condense into visible water droplets. This process creates the cloud’s characteristic shape: thicker in the middle, thinner at the edges, and resembling a UFO.

Since lenticular clouds look like one or more convex lenses, they are sometimes misinterpreted as flying saucers or Unidentified Flying Objects, and are therefore commonly known as “flying saucer clouds”. The Observatory notes that while such clouds do not appear frequently in Hong Kong, they tend to form more readily in mountainous areas where hills disrupt the airflow.

The lenticular clouds. Photo source: FB image

After the Observatory shared the post on social media, netizens responded enthusiastically, uploading their own photographs of “UFO clouds."

Hong Kong cinema showcased at Five Flavours Asian Film Festival in Poland

The Hong Kong Economic and Trade Office, Berlin (HKETO Berlin) supports the Five Flavours Asian Film Festival held in Warsaw, Poland, from November 10 to December 6 (Warsaw time).

This year's festival showcases 10 Hong Kong films. In addition to two recent films, "Montages of a Modern Motherhood" and "Another World", the festival has curated a retrospective programme featuring eight classic works by the director and producer Tsui Hark. The screenings are sponsored by the Cultural and Creative Industries Development Agency of the Culture, Sports and Tourism Bureau and the Film Development Fund.

Speaking before the screening of the opening film "A Chinese Ghost Story" produced by Tsui Hark on November 12, the Director of HKETO Berlin, Mr Indiana Wong, highlighted the richness and diversity of Hong Kong cinema. "From action and martial arts to comedy, drama, and socially conscious films, Hong Kong filmmakers have continually pushed creative boundaries while capturing the spirit of Hong Kong. I invite film and creative professionals to come to Hong Kong, and together we can create quality productions."

HKETO Berlin hosted a reception after the screening, attended by about 200 guests from the business and cultural sectors. Mr Wong took the opportunity to introduce the latest developments in Hong Kong. He also shared that, according to the Chief Executive's 2026 Policy Address, the Support Unit for Non-local Film Productions will be set up to provide one-stop services for Chinese Mainland and overseas film crews filming in Hong Kong, attracting more quality film productions to promote Hong Kong.

During the visit, Mr Wong also met with a local chamber of commerce, journalists, and a start-up organisation to promote the advantages of Hong Kong and exchange views on the latest developments and collaboration opportunities.

About HKETO Berlin

HKETO Berlin is the official representative of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region Government in commercial relations and other economic and trade matters in Germany as well as Austria, Czechia, Hungary, Poland, the Slovak Republic, Slovenia and Switzerland.
